clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive defect of the DDC gene; the enzyme decarboxylates both L-DOPA to dopamine and 5-hydroxytryptophan to serotonin, so it causes combined deficiency of catecholamines (dopamine, noradrenaline, adrenaline) and serotonin.
Oculogyric crises, episodic sustained conjugate upward or lateral eye deviation with distress and dystonic posturing, often worsening through the day, are the clinical hallmark.
Typical infantile presentation combines axial hypotonia with limb hypertonia and dystonia, hypokinesia, developmental delay, irritability and feeding difficulty.
Prominent autonomic dysfunction includes ptosis, pupillary abnormalities, nasal congestion, excessive sweating, temperature instability, hypoglycaemia and gastrointestinal dysmotility.
Diagnosis rests on CSF neurotransmitter metabolites showing low homovanillic acid and 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid with raised 3-O-methyldopa, L-DOPA and 5-hydroxytryptophan.
Supportive findings are reduced plasma AADC enzyme activity and biallelic DDC variants; a founder splice variant is common in East Asian populations.
Symptoms often show a diurnal pattern and are frequently misdiagnosed as epilepsy, cerebral palsy or a mitochondrial disorder.

Because pyridoxal phosphate is the enzyme cofactor, management may combine dopamine agonists, monoamine-oxidase inhibitors and vitamin B6; putaminal AAV-based gene therapy is now available and can improve motor milestones.
reference.pathophysiology: AADC, encoded by DDC, is a pyridoxal-phosphate-dependent enzyme catalysing the final step of monoamine neurotransmitter synthesis, converting L-DOPA to dopamine and 5-hydroxytryptophan to serotonin. Loss of function therefore simultaneously depletes dopaminergic, noradrenergic and adrenergic, and serotonergic signalling. Dopamine deficiency produces the hypokinetic-rigid movement disorder and oculogyric crises; loss of noradrenaline and adrenaline underlies autonomic instability; and serotonin deficiency contributes to disturbances of mood, sleep and gut motility. Upstream substrates accumulate and are shunted through alternative routes, generating the diagnostic rise in 3-O-methyldopa. Because the enzyme depends on pyridoxal phosphate, disorders of vitamin B6 metabolism can mimic or modify the phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Tyrosine hydroxylase deficiency and other dopa-responsive dystonias (GTP cyclohydrolase deficiency / Segawa disease)
Sepiapterin reductase deficiency and other tetrahydrobiopterin defects
Dyskinetic cerebral palsy and other static encephalopathies
Epileptic encephalopathy where oculogyric crises are mistaken for seizures
Other monoamine neurotransmitter synthesis or transport defects
additionalInvestigations: CSF neurotransmitter metabolite panel (homovanillic acid, 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid, 3-O-methyldopa, biopterin and neopterin)
DDC gene sequencing and targeted founder-variant testing
Plasma amino acids and vitamin B6 status
Structured trial of pyridoxal phosphate response
Brain MRI, often normal or non-specific, to exclude structural causes
EEG when seizures are suspected, to distinguish them from oculogyric crises
redFlags: Recurrent oculogyric crises with an autonomic storm (sweating, temperature swings, cardiovascular instability)
Episodes of hypoglycaemia or hypotensive collapse
Apnoea or respiratory compromise during crises
reference.prognosis: The severe classic phenotype causes major motor disability and carries a risk of early death, though autonomic crises and comorbidities are treatable; putaminal gene therapy and optimised pharmacotherapy can yield meaningful motor gains.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing oculogyric crises as epileptic seizures and starting antiseizure drugs.
Attributing the picture to cerebral palsy and not sending CSF neurotransmitter studies.
Interpreting CSF metabolites without age-appropriate reference ranges or correct rostrocaudal sampling.
Using standard L-DOPA replacement and expecting benefit, when the block is downstream of L-DOPA so dopamine agonists are used instead.
references: Inborn errors of metabolism reference texts
management: Putaminal gene therapy delivering the DDC gene is the emerging disease-directed treatment, capable of meaningful motor gains
Pharmacotherapy to augment residual monoamine signalling, using dopamine agonists, monoamine oxidase inhibitors and pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6)
Anticholinergic agents to relieve dystonia and reduce oculogyric crises
Supportive management of autonomic instability, treating temperature dysregulation, blood-pressure lability, excessive sweating and hypoglycaemia
Nutritional support for feeding difficulty and gastrointestinal dysmotility, with gastrostomy feeding where needed
Recognise and abort oculogyric crises, distinguishing them from seizures on clinical grounds and EEG
Offer genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive DDC disorder, with confirmatory testing and family screening including the East Asian founder variant
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across metabolic medicine, neurology, physiotherapy and speech and language therapy
